title: A single-deployment Primitive Instance can encode a permanently repeatable process, as Keel's Root Edit Instance does
content:
A.6.1.1.3.2.2.2.1.4 and A.6.1.1.3.2.2.2.4 both state that "because the Root Edit Primitive is deployed only once, no further Instances of the Primitive can be Invoked," and the Primitive carries exactly one `Active` Instance. Yet A.6.1.1.3.2.2.2.2.1.1 says its parameters "are fully specified by the Operational Process Definition," and that definition (A.6.1.1.3.2.2.2.2.1.2) contains the full Routine, Non-Routine and Emergency protocols for amending the Keel Artifact — a process meant to run indefinitely.

So "Instance" does not mean "occurrence of an event." A single-deployment Instance is better read as a *standing capability*: invoked once to install the machinery, thereafter operated continuously under its own process definition. Individual Root Edits are executions of the Instance's protocol, not new Instances.

This resolves what otherwise looks like a contradiction between a one-shot Primitive and an ongoing governance function, and it explains why the Instance-level skeleton contains an Operational Process Definition at all: some Primitives finish (Agent Creation), while others install a process that never finishes.

The practical consequence for a reader is that Instance count says nothing about activity. Keel's amendment process has run or will run many times through an Instance whose status will read `Active` forever.
description: The Root Edit Primitive is 'deployed only once' with no further Invocations possible, yet its one Instance's Operational Process Definition is the standing protocol for every future amendment.
